meta.title: Load Balancing
meta.summary: One front door for many servers — and the rules for who gets which request.

goals.text: Why a pool of servers needs one front door
Health checks that route around failure
Removing the load balancer as a SPOF

steps.title: Three servers, one address
steps.body:
We scaled out to three servers — but users only know one address, the one in DNS. Every request lands on Server B while A and C sit idle.

The extra hardware bought us nothing. We need a single front door that spreads requests across all of them.

callout.text: Adding servers only helps if traffic actually reaches them.

steps.title: Put a load balancer in front
steps.body:
A [[load balancer]] (LB) becomes the one public address of the service. Clients connect to it; it forwards each request to one of the servers behind it and relays the answer back.

Servers can now come and go without clients ever knowing.

callout.text: The servers behind a load balancer are called its **pool** (or target group).

changes: ~ Users now talk to the LB, not to servers

steps.title: Round robin: take turns
steps.body:
How does the LB choose? The simplest rule is [[round robin]]: A, then B, then C, then A again. Watch the requests go out in turn.

It’s cheap and fair — as long as the servers are equally powerful and every request costs about the same.

callout.text: **Weighted** round robin gives bigger servers a bigger share, e.g. A : B : C = 2 : 1 : 1.

changes: ~ Slowed down so you can follow each request

steps.title: When requests aren’t equal
steps.body:
Real traffic is lumpy. Loading a page takes 5 ms; exporting a year of reports takes 5 seconds. Round robin counts *requests*, not *work*.

Here every third request is heavy (the big squares), and by luck of the rotation they all land on Server B. It drowns while A and C coast.

callout.text: Round robin has no idea how busy a server actually is.

steps.title: Least connections
steps.body:
With [[least connections]], the LB tracks how many requests each server is busy with and sends the next one to the least busy.

A server stuck on slow work holds more open connections, so it automatically receives less new work. The load evens out.

callout.text: Other strategies: **least response time**, **IP hash** (same client → same server) and **power of two choices** (pick two at random, use the less busy).

steps.title: Health checks route around failure
steps.body:
Every few seconds the LB probes each server — say `GET /health`. A server that misses several checks in a row is pulled out of the pool; once it recovers, it’s put back.

Server C just crashed, and users didn’t notice a thing. In the last lesson, a dead server meant errors for a quarter of them.

callout.text: Health checks plus spare servers mean no single server is a single point of failure any more.

changes: ~ C taken out of the pool

steps.title: Who balances the balancer?
steps.body:
We removed one single point of failure and created another. Every request now passes through one load balancer — when it dies, so does everything behind it.

The servers are perfectly healthy. Nobody can reach them.

callout.text: Anything that every request depends on must itself be redundant.

steps.title: Add a standby
steps.body: Run two load balancers: an **active** one serving traffic and a **passive** standby. They share a [[virtual IP]] (VIP) — the address clients actually use — and exchange heartbeats every second.

callout.text: Cloud load balancers (AWS ELB, Google Cloud LB…) do this for you: they run redundantly across machines and zones.

steps.title: Failover in seconds
steps.body:
The active LB dies. The standby notices the missing heartbeats, claims the virtual IP and starts forwarding traffic.

Clients keep using the same address. At worst, a few in-flight requests are retried.

callout.text: This pattern — **active–passive failover** — protects databases, caches and queues too.

changes: ~ VIP moved to the new active LB

steps.title: Route by what’s in the request
steps.body:
Load balancers come in two kinds. A **layer 4** balancer only sees IP addresses and ports, and forwards whole connections. A **layer 7** balancer reads the HTTP request itself.

That lets it route by path: `/api/*` to the API servers, `/images/*` to a separate image service — each pool scaled and deployed on its own.

callout.text: L7 balancers can also route by host name, header or cookie, terminate TLS, and add caching or compression.

steps.title: Case: deploying without downtime
steps.body:
Time to ship version 2. A [[rolling deploy]] updates one server at a time: the load balancer first **drains** it — no new requests, but in-flight ones finish — then it’s updated, passes its health check and rejoins.

Here C is already on v2, B is draining, and A waits its turn. Users never see an error.

callout.text: Blue-green deploys go further: bring up a full v2 pool, then switch the load balancer over at once — and back, if anything looks wrong.

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• A load balancer gives a pool of servers **one stable address**.
• **Round robin** is simple; **least connections** adapts to uneven work.
• **Health checks** pull dead servers out of the pool automatically.
• The LB must be redundant too: **active–passive** with a shared VIP.
• **L7** balancers route by path; **draining** enables zero-downtime deploys.

callout.text: Next up: **Stateless Services** — what breaks when a user’s next request lands on a different server.
